statementIssues.note: The two-player Australian football glycogen sentence cites no retained claim (C24 was removed). It is accurate to Routledge 2018 (115 vs 98 min, 12.2 vs 11.2 km, pre-match glycogen 656 vs 544), but it is uncited in the brief. 'Drawing on a two-game week study' inherits the C32 misattribution.

'The pooled hydration analysis was not significant' is true: the abstract gives p = 0.24 for 10 studies. But none of the cited claims (C7, C9) state it, because C30 was removed, so readers cannot trace it to an excerpt.
'The glycogen data come from only 2 Australian football forwards' cites C11, C21 and C23, none of which is the Routledge source. It is accurate but mis-linked.

The tart cherry tension leaves out the positive soccer study (Bell et al. 2016, 16 players) that the same RL review describes as faster recovery with tart cherry. The review calls the findings 'equivocal', so the brief presents the tension more one-sidedly than the source.
The risk-of-bias wording is ambiguous; see the claim verdict.

tierNote: Limited fits. The evidence is indirect: an expert-opinion statement, elite male soccer and rugby cohorts, a two-player case report and laboratory studies. The brief admits the tension on polyphenols and hydration. recommendedDirection is null and actions are framed as options, with untested advice labeled as professional judgment.
usefulnessNote: Gives a performance dietitian concrete, sourced starting ranges (6-8 g/kg between congested fixtures, ~1 g/kg/h for 4 h after a match), food-safety and gut-tolerance tactics, a narrow supplement stance and travel-scheduling levers, all with honest caveats about transferability. It is long for a two-minute read. Subgroup individualization (low-minute and returning athletes) rests mostly on professional judgment.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When the critic pass removes a claim, also remove or re-source every statement sentence that depended only on that claim, rather than keeping the sentence uncited.
Check that each statement sentence naming a specific source or statistic cites a claim from that source.
When a source attaches a recommendation to a cited study with 'nonetheless' or similar, do not describe the recommendation as drawn from that study.
For evidence tension, include positive findings reported in the same source passage, not only the null ones.
Phrase quality-scale results unambiguously (for example 'low methodological quality scores'), not 'low on risk of bias'.
